To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people’s immediate reactions to rejection are similar across different forms and (2) these immediate reactions are followed by a set of 3 distinct motives (relational, contextual, and individual difference) that determine people’s behavioral reactions to rejection.

(1) rejection is associated with negative affect and lowered sense of self-worth; (2) people respond to rejection in 3 different ways: by seeking social support, by attacking their rejector, and by avoiding the situation; (3) these 3 different types of reactions to rejection are predicted by different construals of rejection (e.g., whether rejection is seen as an attack on the self, an attack on the social relationship, or a threat to belonging); and (4)
people’s immediate reactions to rejection are similar across diverse forms of rejection, but their longer-term reactions vary depending on their construals of rejection experiences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social psychological processes that underlie people's reactions to social rejection, discrimination, and stigmatizaiton, and their implications for well-being and behavior.
the ways in which people’s social relationships are influenced by the threat of rejection.
the ways in which people’s responses to rejection unfold in time.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the multimotive model of reactions to rejection is a very useful framework for the understanding of the reactions to rejection and other forms of interpersonal rejection.

the multimotive model provides a framework for integrating the literature on rejection, ostracism and stigmatization and offers new insights into the processes underlying people’s reactions to social rejection and exclusion.
this article is very informative, and I would recommend that anyone interested in the field of social psychology should read it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the more we understand how people respond to rejection, discrimination, and other forms of social exclusion and stigmatization, the better able we are to design interventions to reduce the negative effects of these experiences and promote positive social relationships.
we have developed a model of the psychological consequences of rejection, discrimination, stigmatization, and ostracism.
people’s reactions to rejection are not only immediate but also multifaceted, dynamic, and highly context dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people’s reactions to rejection are not a unitary response.
the way people think about rejection experiences is what determines the nature of their responses to these experiences.
the way we react to rejection depends on our motives for reacting in particular ways.
